title: Meet-in-the-Middle Compilation of the $[\mathrm{CNOT}]$ Class with Fibonacci Anyons
abstract: Compilation of two-qubit Fibonacci anyon gates is complicated by leakage ($\ell$) from the four-dimensional computational sector to the fifth state of the fusion space. We construct a GPU pipeline to find low-leakage representatives of the $[\text{CNOT}]$ class on different subsets of the braid group.   We exhaustively explore the full positive five-generator alphabet up to $L=21$ with minimal leakage $\ell\sim10^{-3}$ and error $d_{[\text{CNOT}]}\sim 10^{-8}$ on it. To reach larger lengths, the search space is successively narrowed to three-generator, boundary-$σ_3$, and palindromic braids, and by considering only the Garside left normal form. These optimizations allow us to reach $L=72$. For $L=69$, a braid with $\ell\sim10^{-10}$ and $d_{[\text{CNOT}]}\sim 10^{-10}$ is found.   In addition to directly enumerating optimal braids, we proved that $\ell\in\mathbb Z[\varphi]$, and any nonzero leakage obeys an exponential lower bound in the braid length, and obtained the limit laws $F_{3,\infty}(\ell)=\ell^2$ and $F_{5,\infty}(\ell)=\ell^4$ for our sets. Using asymptotics for the distribution function $F$, we showed that for sufficiently long braids, the asymptotics of exhaustive search are better than the asymptotics of random sampling for finding low-leakage braids.
summary: This work develops advanced computational and mathematical techniques to find high-fidelity implementations of the CNOT gate using Fibonacci anyons. By employing a Meet-in-the-Middle search pipeline, the authors push the achievable braid length significantly while proving that exhaustive search methods provide superior asymptotic guarantees compared to random sampling for minimizing leakage.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of finding low-leakage representatives for the $[\mathrm{CNOT}]$ class of two-qubit gates using Fibonacci anyons in topological quantum computation.
main_result: They successfully extended the exhaustive search for optimal braids to length $L=72$ and proved that exhaustive search asymptotics outperform random sampling for finding low-leakage gates.
method: The authors combine a Meet-In-The-Middle (MITM) GPU pipeline with exhaustive search techniques, alongside rigorous mathematical analysis of leakage distributions via limit laws.
model_or_system: The model is topological quantum computation utilizing Fibonacci anyons, whose dynamics are governed by the braid group. The quality of the gate is assessed by minimizing leakage ($\ell$) from the computational sector to higher fusion space states.
key_observables: Leakage ($\ell$), error distance ($d_{[\mathrm{CNOT}]}$), and the dimension of fusion spaces ($	ext{dim } V_{	au 	imes n}$).
important_parameters: Braid length ($L$), the golden ratio ($\varphi$), and the specific dimensions $d=3$ and $d=5$ related to the fusion space.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the support of the generators generates a dense subgroup of the projective unitary group $PU(d)$ to apply Haar measure convergence theorems.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes reference limit laws $F_{3,\infty}(\ell)=\ell^2$ and $F_{5,\infty}(\ell)=\ell^4$ derived from distribution function analysis.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (leakage in $[\mathrm{CNOT}]$) to developing advanced search algorithms (MITM, exhaustive search), followed by rigorous mathematical proofs regarding leakage bounds and asymptotic distribution laws.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical analysis of leakage and the comparison of search algorithms provide deep theoretical tools for assessing the feasibility and error scaling of topological quantum computation protocols.

Figure 3: Exhaustive leakage CDFs for selected lengths in the positive restricted alphabet {σ1, σ2, σ3} (left) and the positive full alphabet {σ1, . . . , σ5} (right). Every word of each displayed length is counted with multiplicity. As the length increases, the finite discrete distributions approach the respective Haar limits F∞(ℓ) = ℓ2 and F∞(ℓ) = ℓ4 proved in Appendix B. The black dotted lines mark ℓ= φ−1. The finite-length curves were obtained by exhaustive enumeration in production machine arithmetic; they illustrate convergence but are not used to prove Haar mixing.
